message.content:
In computer‑vision pipelines, “purple” is usually treated just like any other color but is chosen deliberately for its rarity in natural imagery. Because most real‑world scenes contain very little pure purple, it becomes a convenient **marker color**:

| Use | Why purple is useful |
|-----|----------------------|
| **Marker / fiducial detection** | A camera can quickly isolate a purple patch or sticker using simple thresholding in HSV or Lab space. Since few objects naturally contain this hue, false positives are low. |
| **Background for segmentation** | When training a segmentation network, a uniform purple background guarantees that the network learns to ignore that color, helping it focus on foreground objects. |
| **Labeling / annotation** | Annotators often paint objects with distinct colors (red, green, blue, purple, yellow, cyan). Purple is one of the few hues that is easily distinguishable from the typical RGB palette used in many datasets. |
| **Color‑coded overlays** | In visualization tools, purple is used to highlight regions of interest (e.g., bounding boxes, heat‑maps) because it stands out against common backgrounds. |

In practice, you would convert your image to a color space that separates hue from intensity (HSV, Lab, YCbCr), then apply a threshold around the purple hue range (≈ 260–280° in HSV). After thresholding, you can use morphological operations to clean up the mask and feed it into downstream tasks such as object tracking or pose estimation.
